content:
The salt had a way of getting into everything. It settled in the creases of Elias’s knuckles, crusted in the corners of his eyes, and seemed to weigh down his very soul. For thirty years, he had tended the Gull’s Beak Lighthouse, a jagged tooth of granite jutting out into the North Atlantic. His life was measured in rotations of the great Fresnel lens and the rhythmic crash of waves against the rocks below.

It was a Tuesday in late November, the kind of day where the sky and the sea merged into a single, bruised purple. The storm had passed, leaving behind a debris field of kelp, driftwood, and the occasional plastic bottle. Elias was walking the shoreline, his boots squelching in the wet sand, when a glint of green caught his eye.

It wasn’t plastic. It was glass, thick and old, half-buried in a tangle of seaweed.

He dug it out with his gloved hands. The bottle was dark emerald, sealed with wax that had hardened into a black, waxy lump. Inside, rolled tightly, was a scrap of parchment.

Elias carried it back to the lighthouse, his heart beating a strange, irregular rhythm against his ribs. He placed the bottle on his workbench, under the warm glow of the oil lamp. With a small knife, he chipped away the wax. It crumbled like dry earth. He pulled out the paper, unrolling it with trembling fingers.

The handwriting was shaky, faded by time and moisture, but legible.

*“To whoever finds this,*

*My name is Arthur Penhaligon. I was the keeper of the Gull’s Beak Light, forty years before you. I write this not as a warning, but as a confession.*

*On the night of October 14, 1983, I saw a ship. Not a ghost ship, but a real one, the *Marisol*. It was struggling against the rocks. I had the chance to signal them away, to guide them into the safe channel. But I was tired. So tired. And I was angry at the world for making me live here, alone, forgotten. I let the light dim for just ten minutes. Just long enough for them to think the coast was clear.*

*They crashed. I heard the screams. I never told anyone. I lived with the silence for the rest of my life
